questions.question: What is the correct syntax for an f-string that includes the variable `name`?
questions.explanation: F-strings require an `f` before the opening quote. The correct syntax is `f"Hello {name}"`. Without the `f`, Python treats it as a regular string with literal curly braces.
questions.terminalHint: 💡 Try this in your terminal! Type: `name = "Alice"; print(f"Hello {name}")`

questions.question: Look at this code: `name = "Sam"; age = 25`. Which f-string will print "Sam is 25 years old"?
questions.explanation: To use variables in an f-string, put them inside curly braces `{}`. So `{name}` becomes "Sam" and `{age}` becomes 25, giving us "Sam is 25 years old".
questions.terminalHint: 💡 Try all options in your terminal! See which one uses the variables correctly.

questions.question: Which of these is an advantage of f-strings over concatenation?
options: F-strings are faster to write and easier to read
F-strings only work with string variables
F-strings require importing a special module
questions.explanation: F-strings are cleaner, faster to write, and easier to read than concatenation. They automatically convert other data types to strings, can include expressions directly, and don't require any imports in modern Python (3.6+).
